how_it_wins:
The table will look at the commander, decide you are the Yawgmoth deck, and point their removal at him. Half the time, let them. He recasts from the command zone, his job in the grind is cards — that ability costs no mana at all, so it runs through a tax, through a lock, and at instant speed on somebody else's end step — and he arrives on turn four in 7,188 of 10,000 goldfished games without any help from you. But know which kill you are on before you shrug. The two Gravecrawler loops and the Exquisite Blood pair never name him; the Nest engine, the Mikaeus line and the undying pair all need him standing. Exactly three cards carry him through a removal spell — Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina, Malakir Rebirth. Those are engine-turn cards. Never spend one for value.

You have six verified shapes, and every one of them ends the whole table at once — so never aim a kill at a seat. Two are unbounded: stack 009 funds itself with Treasure, and stack 011 pays nothing at all and gains you a life a lap. Stack 012 is lethal precisely because it cannot stop. Two spend your library, and spend it with room to spare: stack 010 needs 39 activations of the 59 you get, stack 014 kills in about 30 of the roughly 55 available. And the sixth is the one you will actually play most: Nest of Scarabs plus any drain, rotations stacked across turns, Yawgmoth doing the counting.

Here is the gap you pilot around. The enabler layers are enormous — by turn 10 you have drawn a drain 82.3% of the time, renewable fodder 82.3%, a free sacrifice outlet 78.5%, an ignition source 73.8%. The named kills read tiny beside that: 13.5% for the Nest engine unassisted, single digits for everything else. Read those one at a time and never add them up. The machine will be running; your turns go to hunting the one missing card. That is what five tutors are for — a tutor is what carries the Exquisite Blood kill from 6.6% to 42.6% — so never cast one for value either.

A wrath is not what beats you. Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat, Blood Artist and The Meathook Massacre all get paid when your creatures die, and Gravecrawler and Reassembling Skeleton rebuild cheaper than anyone at the table. What beats you is a permanent you cannot remove: one card in the 99 destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it only reaches enchantments. So stop planning to answer the hate and pick the kill that dodges it — Exquisite Blood needs no graveyard, no outlet, no recursion and no commander. Deploy in the order that costs you least when it gets answered, put the drain down last, and say bracket 4 at Rule 0 — four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinite records force it — then go play exactly the deck you just described.

combo_lines.002: The clause is “up to one target creature”, and targets are locked in when the ability is activated (CR 115.1c) — the Insect the Nest is about to make does not yet exist to be chosen. Protection from Humans keeps Yawgmoth off his own list (CR 702.16b). So the moment the opponent's creature is dead, every legal target is one of your own tokens: two bodies leave, one comes back. The holding: this engine draws cards and then stops. It is not a kill, and no ordering makes it one.
combo_lines.003: Three permissions, and not a restriction among them. You choose which creature pays “Sacrifice another creature” (CR 601.2h), “up to one target” permits choosing none (CR 115.6), and a leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back at the board as it was (CR 603.10a). Nothing here can take Zulaport Cutthroat away from you against your will. He survives every iteration and is spent as the deliberate final sacrifice, where his own trigger banks the seventh drain. The holding: seven drains, and the table lives through them.
combo_lines.004: Four words decide the case. Blood Artist reads “target player loses 1 life” — one seat per trigger, chosen as the trigger goes on the stack — where the drains that end games read each opponent. The engine also finishes by eating its own payoff: protection bars the commander as a target and “another creature” bars him as the sacrifice, so the Artist is the last legal thing left to point at. The holding: eight triggers, eight life, against a pod holding 160. The arithmetic divides by four and never recovers.
combo_lines.005: CR 119.9 is the clause, and it is a small one: an event that gains you 0 life is not a life-gain event at all. An Insect killed by its own -1/-1 counter dies at toughness 0, so South Wind Avatar's dies-trigger resolves for nothing and the second ability never fires. The holding: eight dies-triggers, seven drains. The Avatar's 4 toughness is what does the real work here, absorbing counters that a 1/1 drainer could not take.
combo_lines.006: CR 122.6 is broader than it first reads: a reference to putting counters on an object covers an object given counters as it enters, not only counters placed on something already sitting there. Persist names no player, so 122.6a makes you the one placing it — which is precisely what Nest of Scarabs asks for. The holding: the Nest triggers and you get an Insect, even though the returned Fume Spitter is back in the graveyard before that trigger reaches the stack. It had already triggered.
combo_lines.008: Savour the order of operations. A cost is paid after the ability is already the topmost object on the stack (CR 602.2a into 601.2h), so the trigger the sacrifice causes lands above it and resolves first. One activation paid with a token therefore pays Mirkwood Bats twice: once for the sacrifice, once for the creation two resolutions later. One caveat for the record — a token killed by its own counter is put into the graveyard by the game rather than sacrificed by you (CR 704.5f), and pays the Bats on creation only.
combo_lines.009: The elegant clause is CR 113.6f: an ability that modifies which zones its own card may be cast from functions in that zone. Gravecrawler's permission is therefore live in the graveyard every iteration, its Zombie condition met by Warren Soultrader, whom “another creature” keeps permanently out of the loop. Each Treasure is an artifact and not a creature, so it funds the recast without restriction. The holding: the loop pays for itself, one drain a lap, and nothing on this board brings it to an end.
combo_lines.010: CR 704.5q is the crux — a permanent holding both a +1/+1 and a -1/-1 counter loses one of each to state-based actions. So the commander's counter does not shrink an undying body. It strips the +1/+1 that undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again. The holding: the alternation is real, and the loop is finite, because the draw is mandatory. It needs 39 activations against the 59 the library permits, a margin of 20. One trap the record is explicit about: Viscera Seer's own sacrifice places no counter, and only the commander's counter can strip an undying return, so a mid-loop activation costs a body that cannot be re-armed.
combo_lines.011: One line of rules text carries the whole thing. Phyrexian Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability (CR 605.1a) and never uses the stack (CR 605.3b) — the {B} is in the pool before anyone receives priority, and there is nothing to respond to. Sacrificing Gravecrawler refunds exactly the mana that recasts him, with Carrion Feeder holding the Zombie condition and never being the sacrifice. The holding: unbounded, and free — each lap costs nothing and gains you a life.
combo_lines.012: Counsel's favourite kind of question: the loop is mandatory — neither card says “may” — so does the game simply end in a draw? No, and CR 732.1b is why. A draw requires a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and this one cannot, because every cycle takes a life from every opponent. There is a way to stop, which is all CR 104.4b asks. The holding: drain 40 takes all four opponents to 0, state-based actions are checked before the resulting triggers reach the stack, and they leave together (CR 704.5a). You are still there, so you win (CR 104.2a).
combo_lines.014: The clause that decides this case is one the deck usually loves: "and draw a card" — no "may" anywhere in it, and a resolving ability's instructions must be followed (CR 608.2c). The alternation itself is genuine and elegant: each undying return leaves a +1/+1 counter, the commander's -1/-1 annihilates it by state-based action (CR 704.5q), and the body dies counter-free again, forever in principle. But "unbounded" is refuted on the record, because every activation is a mandatory draw against a library of roughly 55, and the draw after the last one loses the game (CR 121.4, 704.5b). The holding: library-bounded at ~55 activations — and the bound never saves the table, because each two-activation cycle takes 2 from every opponent and 4 from the Messenger's target at net-zero life to the pilot, so ~30 activations end the pod with ~25 draws of margin.

card_roles.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: Cast him to draw — the ability costs no mana at all, so run it at instant speed on the turn before yours and convert spare bodies into cards. In the grind let the table kill him, he recasts; on the engine turn he is the hub of three of your six verified kills, and that turn is what the Greaves and the save spells exist for.
card_roles.Nest of Scarabs: Every counter you place becomes a body, so point the commander's counters at their creatures when you need the board clear and at your own when you need fodder. Count by creatures touched, not counters placed — one proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures hands you three Insects.
card_roles.Mirkwood Bats: Get it down before you start converting tokens, not after: one commander activation paid with a token pays this drain twice, once going out and once coming back. Its 2/3 body also absorbs two counters and lives, which buys you activations a 1/1 cannot.
card_roles.Ayara, First of Locthwain: Play her the moment your first three lands are black and let every black creature that follows chip the whole table. Keep one spare black body back for her tap-to-draw rather than feeding everything to the commander.
card_roles.Bastion of Remembrance: Treat this as a combo piece, not a value enchantment — it is the drain three of your verified kills route through, so resolve it on the turn you mean to convert rather than the turn you draw it. It also hands you a free Soldier to eat on arrival.
card_roles.Zulaport Cutthroat: A drain on a body that slots into any recursion kill, and nothing can force you to eat him. Sacrifice him last and on purpose: his own trigger sees his death and banks one more drain.
card_roles.Blood Artist: He hits one seat per trigger where your real finishers hit every opponent at once, so play him for value and never tutor for him as the kill. He is still the best thing to have on the battlefield when somebody wraths.
card_roles.South Wind Avatar: Deathtouch keeps him alive on defence and his toughness soaks counters, but the line that matters is the second one — gain a life, every opponent loses one. Put him beside Exquisite Blood and stop looking for anything else.
card_roles.Exquisite Blood: Your fastest kill and the only one that touches no graveyard, no outlet and no commander, so reach for this shape the moment somebody lands hate on the rest of the deck. The pair comes together on a mean turn 5.1, so play toward it early rather than treating it as a late-game plan.
card_roles.Marauding Blight-Priest: The same each-opponent lifegain trigger on a cheaper body — your second and third shot at the Exquisite Blood kill. Deploy him early, while the table still reads him as a 2/2 that does nothing.
card_roles.Starscape Cleric: Cheap, flies, and carries the lifegain drain. Buy the Offspring copy whenever the mana is spare: two bodies with that trigger means the table loses two life for every life you gain.
card_roles.The Meathook Massacre: Cast it when your board is the one that profits — your creatures dying drains each opponent, theirs dying gains you life, and X scales to whatever has been deployed. This is the wipe you want to be holding, not the one you fear.
card_roles.Grave Pact: Your only repeatable edict and your answer to a creature you cannot target: every sacrifice you were making anyway now costs each opponent a body. Land it before the protected threat arrives, not after.
card_roles.Gravecrawler: The one slot with no substitute — two unbounded kills route through him. Keep a second Zombie on the battlefield at all times so his recast permission stays live, and never let the loop eat that Zombie.
card_roles.Warren Soultrader: A Zombie who turns each sacrifice into a Treasure, and that Treasure exactly pays Gravecrawler's next cast. He satisfies the Zombie condition himself, so sacrifice anything on the board except him.
card_roles.Phyrexian Altar: Your best engine mana: sacrifice for any colour, and it never uses the stack, so nobody gets a window to respond. With Gravecrawler and a spare Zombie the loop costs you nothing to run.
card_roles.Pitiless Plunderer: Every other creature you lose becomes a Treasure, which turns a board wipe into a pile of mana. Four mana looks steep right up until the turn you sacrifice five things.
card_roles.Ashnod's Altar: Free outlet and two colorless whenever you need a body gone at instant speed. Know the limit before you rely on it: colorless does not recast Gravecrawler, so use it for outlet work and bulk mana, never as the loop's fuel.
card_roles.Phyrexian Tower: An outlet, two black mana and a land drop in one slot. Save the activation for the turn the mana matters — you only get it once a turn.
card_roles.Carrion Feeder: One mana, a free outlet, and a Zombie — that last word is why he can stand in the recursion loop and hold Gravecrawler's permission open. He cannot block, so plan your defence elsewhere.
card_roles.Viscera Seer: One mana for a free outlet that filters every draw. Keep her out of the Mikaeus loop mid-stream — her sacrifice places no counter, so it costs a body you cannot re-arm. Save her for the finish.
card_roles.Woe Strider: A free outlet, a Goat to feed it on arrival, and escape from your own graveyard after the table wipes. Three jobs for three mana, and you will use all three.
card_roles.Yahenni, Undying Partisan: The outlet that lives through your own sweepers — sacrifice anything and she is indestructible for the turn. She is also a legal undying body under Mikaeus.
card_roles.Blasting Station: A free outlet that closes from a board no drain can reach, and it untaps every time a creature enters, which with your token production is constantly. Sequence your tokens into it and keep pulling the trigger.
card_roles.Reassembling Skeleton: Pay two, get a body, forever. Hold the mana for it on any turn you have nothing better to do — this is the fodder that never runs out.
card_roles.Butcher Ghoul: Half of the verified undying pair: under the commander he and Geralf's Messenger alternate deaths for as long as your library holds out — stack 014's kill in about 30 activations. On his own he is still a Zombie that dies twice and holds Gravecrawler's recast permission open.
card_roles.Geralf's Messenger: The other half of stack 014's pair, and the seat his enters-trigger points at loses double what the rest of the table does — aim it at whoever is closest to dead. Three black pips and he enters tapped, so cast him on a turn where a tapped body costs you nothing.
card_roles.Stitcher's Supplier: One mana for a Zombie that fills your graveyard coming in and going out. Play it on turn one — your recursion suite wants targets more than you want the 1/1.
card_roles.Bitterblossom: Two mana for a body every upkeep, at a life apiece, for the rest of the game — and it keeps producing while you hold up interaction. Play it on turn two every single time.
card_roles.Grave Titan: Ten power across three bodies, and two more Zombies every time it attacks. This is how an emptied board becomes an engine again, and it is the best thing in your graveyard to reanimate.
card_roles.Sedgemoor Witch: Ward makes her expensive to answer and every instant or sorcery you cast hands you a Pest. Those Pests gain you life when they die, which your lifegain drains are watching for.
card_roles.Black Market Connections: Take the mode the board is short of every first main phase — a Treasure, a card, or a 3/2 — and pay the life without flinching. That flexibility beats a fixed draw engine in a deck that needs a different resource every turn.
card_roles.Necropotence: Life is your cheapest resource in a deck whose loops finish at 80, so spend it hard. Decide how many you want before you start paying: the cards arrive at your end step, and a turn spent overpaying is a turn you cannot cast them.
card_roles.Skullclamp: One mana, and every 1/1 you own becomes two cards. With Bitterblossom, Nest of Scarabs and Grave Titan all making bodies, equip it the moment you have a token you are happy to kill.
card_roles.Deadly Dispute: Instant-speed conversion: a creature already in the removal crosshairs becomes two cards and a Treasure. Cast it in response to the removal, never before.
card_roles.Plumb the Forbidden: Your insurance against a wrath or a targeted exile — sacrifice as many creatures as you like in response and copy it for each. Keep two mana up any turn a sweeper is live.
card_roles.Sinister Gnarlbark: A card and a free counter at every end step, which with the Nest out is a free Insect every turn as well. Three mana for ignition you never have to pay for again.
card_roles.Insatiable Avarice: Three mana either way — one mode sets the top of your library, the other draws three for 3 life — and five mana buys both on one cast. Take the tutor mode when you are a piece short and both when you are short and out of cards.
card_roles.Demonic Tutor: Two mana, any card, straight to hand. When a kill is one piece short this is the shortest road there — do not spend it on a land.
card_roles.Vampiric Tutor: One mana at instant speed for the exact card you need, on top of your library. Cast it at the end of the turn before you need it, because it costs you a draw step.
card_roles.Beseech the Mirror: Bargain something you were going to sacrifice anyway and the four-or-less piece arrives free. Hold this one for the turn you want the tutor and the kill to happen together.
card_roles.Diabolic Intent: The additional cost is a creature dying, which every payoff on your board is already waiting for. Sacrifice into your drains and you get the tutor at a discount you were collecting anyway.
card_roles.Persist: Two mana returns a nonlegendary body carrying a counter — a creature and an Insect on one card when the Nest is out. Point it at something worth more than the counter takes off it.
card_roles.Victimize: One sacrifice, two bodies back tapped. It pays every layer at once: a death trigger going out and two arrivals coming in.
card_roles.Animate Dead: Two mana for the best creature in any graveyard, theirs included. The -1/-0 never matters when the body's job is to die again.
card_roles.Phyrexian Reclamation: Two mana and 2 life, at instant speed, as often as you like — this is how you rebuild through hate aimed at the battlefield. Buy the answered piece back on their end step.
card_roles.Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: Six mana turns every non-Human you own into a body that comes back, and beside the commander that alternation is a kill. Cast him when you can still hold something up, because the loop itself asks for no more mana.
card_roles.Massacre Girl, Known Killer: Wither makes your combat damage into counters, which is removal, ignition and Nest fuel from one attack step. Every small creature an opponent loses draws you a card on top of it.
card_roles.Skinrender: Three counters on arrival: kill their creature outright, or aim it at your own body and collect three Insects. Choose by what the board is short of, and it is usually bodies.
card_roles.Soul Snuffers: A counter on every creature sweeps the small stuff and lights the Nest across your whole board in one cast. Yes, it hits yours — that is normally why you are casting it.
card_roles.Fume Spitter: One mana, sacrifices itself, places a counter — the cheapest ignition you own and a death trigger in the same card. Play it turn one when the alternative is nothing.
card_roles.Black Sun's Zenith: The only sweeper you have that leaves counters behind, which makes it the only sweeper the Nest can see. Set X to what kills their board and let your drains collect on yours.
card_roles.Feed the Swarm: The one card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it only reaches enchantments. Hold it for the permanent that genuinely stops you rather than the first irritating thing you see.
card_roles.Deadly Rollick: Free while your commander is on the battlefield, and it exiles rather than destroys. This is the best argument for keeping Yawgmoth around on the turns you are not using him.
card_roles.Fatal Push: One mana kills a two-drop, or a four-drop the moment anything of yours has left the battlefield this turn. In this deck that condition is on every turn — sacrifice something first and swing the ceiling up.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Zero equip pulls a piece out of the crosshairs and lets an outlet work the turn it lands. Move the boots off before you need to target that creature yourself.
card_roles.Supernatural Stamina: One mana saves a creature from removal and hands you a free death trigger on the way through. Keep it up on any turn your drain is out and the table has mana open.
card_roles.Gray Merchant of Asphodel: Count your devotion before you cast him and pick the turn the table is already low — in a list this full of black pips the number gets ugly fast. He is a Zombie for Gravecrawler and a reanimation target besides.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless on turn one is why your commander sometimes arrives on turn two. Play it the moment you see it and never think about it again.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana out of a land for 2 damage a tap. Colorless is a genuine constraint here, so spend it on the generic half of a cost and leave the pips to a Swamp.
card_roles.Dark Ritual: One black into three, once. Spend it on the turn that changes the game — a turn-one Bitterblossom, a turn-two commander — and never on a turn you were merely ahead anyway.
card_roles.Castle Locthwain: Untapped black as long as you control a Swamp, which here is nearly always. Its draw costs life equal to your hand size, so fire it when your hand is almost empty.
card_roles.Cabal Pit: Black mana for a point of damage, and once your graveyard is seven deep it sacrifices itself to shrink a creature. Hold that mode for a blocker you actually need gone.
card_roles.Ifnir Deadlands: Black mana for a life, plus a late-game sink that drops two counters on an opposing creature. That is removal and Nest ignition out of a land slot — keep the Desert around to pay for it.
card_roles.Cabal Coffers: Two mana and a tap for a black per Swamp, which with 21 basics and Urborg out is the biggest tap you will make all game. It counts as one source on paper; play it like several.
card_roles.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: It makes no mana itself and counts for nothing in the source column — what it does is turn every land you own into a Swamp for Cabal Coffers. Get it down early and let the rest of the base improve.
card_roles.Bojuka Bog: A tapped land that exiles a graveyard on arrival. Hold it for the reanimator seat instead of jamming it turn one; a tapped land costs you almost nothing on turn six.
card_roles.Takenuma, Abandoned Mire: Black mana, or channel it away to buy a creature back — cheaper for every legendary creature you control, and you run five. A land that doubles as a recursion spell.
card_roles.Command Tower: Untapped black, no condition, no cost. Nothing here to think about.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: It taps for whatever an opponent's lands could make, which is black often enough to count on. Glance at the table before you build a triple-black turn around it.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, a point of damage a tap. In a deck whose kills finish at 80 life you will pay that all game and smile.
card_roles.Survivors' Encampment: Colorless, or any colour by tapping a spare body, and you generally have one. Tap the creature you were not planning to sacrifice this turn.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped for black, and scries whenever that mana casts a Human or a Cleric. Put it down on a turn you were not going to spend all your mana anyway — with only three taplands in the base, that turn always comes.
card_roles.Agadeem's Awakening // Agadeem, the Unde: Pay the 3 life to have the land side arrive untapped; here that is almost always right. Keep the front face in mind for the turn after a wipe, when it brings your whole curve back at once.
card_roles.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: A land on the turns you are short and a two-life save on the turn your key creature gets targeted. The return is another death trigger for every drain you have out.
card_roles.Swamp: Twenty-one of them, which is why the black count works and why Cabal Coffers does what it does. Lead on a basic and keep the utility lands for turns you can afford to spend on them.
card_roles.Ophiomancer: A deathtouch Snake at the beginning of every upkeep — yours and theirs — so long as the last one is gone. Feed each Snake to an outlet before the next upkeep and one two-drop hands you a body per player per rotation, forever.
card_roles.Pawn of Ulamog: Every nontoken creature you lose banks a Spawn that is both one more body to spend and a sacrifice-for-{C}. Know the limit: colorless pays the generic half of a big turn, never Gravecrawler's {B} — spend the Spawns on casting, and then spend the Spawns.
card_roles.Jet Medallion: One generic off every black spell you cast, which in a deck this cheap means most turns play one spell deeper. It discounts casts, not activations — the commander's ability was already free.
card_roles.Nykthos, Shrine to Nyx: Two mana and a tap for your devotion to black, and in a list where nearly every permanent carries black pips the number climbs fast. On paper it counts for nothing; in play it is the biggest single burst of {B} the base can make — fire it on the turn you mean to dump your hand, not to fix a curve.

mulligan:
Most people mulligan this deck hunting for the commander. Don't. He lands on turn four in 7,188 of 10,000 goldfished games with no help at all, so keep the hand that gives him something to eat, or the hand that wins without him.

Keep a shape, not a card list: something that sacrifices, something to sacrifice, and two to four lands. That is what 9,132 of 10,000 kept hands look like, and from there your turn-3 land drop hits 91.6%. The outlet and the fodder are interchangeable, so stop holding out for the good one. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Woe Strider, Yahenni and Blasting Station all do the outlet job; Bitterblossom, Reassembling Skeleton, Stitcher's Supplier, Ophiomancer and Gravecrawler are every one of them fodder. A free outlet turns up by turn 10 in 78.5% of games — you do not need the specific one in your opener.

Ship the hand that is all payoff, however good it looks. Exquisite Blood, Grave Titan and five lands is a mulligan: mean available mana is 3.908 on turn 4, so a five-drop with nothing under it means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs. Payoffs sit there waiting for an engine nobody built.

One land is a ship unless Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual is sitting next to it. Zero lands is always a ship, and only 284 opening sevens in 10,000 come out that way, so it will hardly ever be the decision in front of you. Ship freely in general — you keep the first seven 81.6% of the time at a mean of 0.222 mulligans, which makes the first one a trade you are allowed to take on instinct. And take the hand with a tutor over the hand with the commander every time: a tutor is what turns a 6.6% kill into a 42.6% one.
upgrades:
Zero. That is the count of artifact answers among all 80 entries, by enumeration of every oracle text in the deck, and it is the number that orders this page. Twelve removal copies sit above Walser's floor, so depth is not the problem — breadth is: two of five interaction classes covered, with Feed the Swarm reaching enchantments only.

The top two entries are the diagnosis's own standing adds. Gate to Phyrexia is two mana, repeats every upkeep, and is the only card on this list that moves the breadth count at all — 2 classes to 3 — which matters because a turn-two Grafdigger's Cage blanks the Gravecrawler recasts under both unbounded kills and every undying return under the Mikaeus and undying-pair lines. Culling the Weak is aimed at the smallest, lowest-rated engine class on the board: fast mana, three cards, drawn in 43.6% of games, the reason the commander lands on turn 2 in only 7.2% of sims. One body becomes BBBB for one mana. Its cost is stated in its entry, not hidden — ramp goes 12 to 13, one over the window. Both carry named natural cuts: Grave Pact and Victimize, one-for-one proposals, not a package.

Ranks three through nine extend architecture that is already verified. Bloodthirsty Conqueror doubles the scarce half of the deck's best commander-free kill — Exquisite Blood is one card drawn 6.6% unassisted, and the Conqueror is the same text on a 5/5 flying deathtoucher, opening three new two-card lines with drains already sleeved. Imp's Mischief is the one entry the protection count credits, 3 to 4, guarding the gate that three of the six kills pay: the commander on the engine turn. Sifter of Skulls and Altar of Dementia thicken the death-to-mana class at 61.2% and the free-outlet class at 78.5% respectively; Drivnod, Nether Traitor and Deathgreeter each buy a measured layer a little more slack.

The tenth, Walking Ballista, closes nothing any counted axis names, and its own entry says so — it is bought entirely on a two-card Mikaeus line nobody has put through the checker. Which is the honest note to end on: not one combo line these ten open is verified. Every one carries "needs a stack scenario", and that is a bill, not a footnote. The floor was recomputed rather than asserted — bracket 4 before, 4 after, on all ten — so nothing on this page changes the Rule 0 conversation.
mana_base:
Thirty-six land copies across 16 entries, and only three enter tapped — two of those always. Twenty-one are basic Swamps, so well over half the base is a single card repeated, and that concentration is exactly why Cabal Coffers counts as one source on paper and behaves like something else entirely at the table.

Pip share and source share both read 1.0. They agree perfectly because there is only one colour here to disagree about, so there is nothing to reconcile — just a count. 33 black land sources against a target of 36, and the whole gap is the three lands that make no counted black at all: Ancient Tomb taps for {C}{C}, Urborg taps for nothing on its own, and Nykthos gets no unconditional credit because its devotion payout is exactly the kind of restriction the counter refuses to price. The analysis puts the caveat plainly, and it is worth quoting: "the target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 36-land deck".

Nonland producers carry 33 up to 41, and the composition matters far more than the total. Ten cards produce; eight of them add black, and not one of the eight does it unconditionally — the rituals are one-shots or the back faces of lands, and Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer, Pawn of Ulamog and Warren Soultrader all want a creature to die first. In this deck that is less credit than it sounds like: creatures die here on schedule. Jet Medallion never shows up in the source column at all, because a discount is not a source — it is one generic off every black spell, which is a different way of being an extra land.

The demand side is mild for a mono-colour deck. 76 black pips across 55 cards, a maximum of 3 on any one card and an effective 2, with the first pip due on turn 1. Double black on curve is what this base is actually asked for, and 33 land sources is comfortably more than that costs: 86.9% on-curve from lands alone, 94.8% once the rocks and dorks are counted — call it eight points bought on credit, with no survival discount taken on the creatures underwriting it.

Development agrees. The land drop hits 99.7% on turn 2, 91.6% on turn 3 and 80.7% on turn 4, with mean available mana of 3.079, 3.908 and 5.230 on turns 3, 4 and 6 against a commander who costs four and lands on a median turn 4. Nothing here is ever stuck on colour. The mana is not the number in this deck worth worrying about.
threat_assessment:
The table has a plan for you, and they made it before you sat down: kill the doctor, the problem goes away. Let them keep it. It is half right, and the wrong half is where your games come from.

Three of your six verified kills never need Yawgmoth on the battlefield — the Soultrader loop (stack 009), the Altar loop (stack 011), Exquisite Blood (stack 012). Three gate on him, including the primary Nest engine (stacks 002 through 004) and both library-bounded lines (stacks 010 and 014). So the rule is phase, not posture. In the grind, trade him cheerfully — he recasts from the command zone and the tax is two mana and a turn. On the engine turn, protect him absolutely.

Your protection is exactly three cards: Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina, Malakir Rebirth. They are engine-turn insurance, nothing else. Never spend one saving a value creature in the mid-game; the turn they exist for is the one where a commander-gated kill is live and the table has mana up.

He lands turn four in 7,188 of 10,000 goldfished games and turn two in 718. Fast mana is three cards — Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb, Dark Ritual — in hand by turn ten in 43.6% of games, so the turn-2 doctor is a windfall, not a plan. Keep the hand that gives him bodies to eat, not the hand that promises him early.

Now the game you will actually play most nights. By turn ten you hold a drain 82.3% of the time, renewable fodder 82.3%, a free outlet 78.5%, an ignition source 73.8% — and your best kill assembles unassisted in 13.5% of games. Read that gap as a job description. Run the value engine, look like the value seat, and dig.

Digging is what he is for. His ability costs no mana and the draw is stapled on, so sacrifice at instant speed on other people's turns and bank cards. Ophiomancer's upkeep Snake and Pawn of Ulamog's Spawn pay him in his own currency without costing you a card — feed him those and keep your hand for pieces.

One feeding rule: Gravecrawler goes in the machine only while a second Zombie is on the battlefield, because the graveyard recast needs a Zombie staring back. With that condition met, sacrifice it freely — it returns for one black, and that permission is the entire reason both unbounded kills exist. As your only Zombie, it is a kill half. Protect it like one.

Tutors: five of them, drawn by turn ten in 61.2% of games, and they take the primary line from 7.5% to 38.9% assembled by turn six — the biggest number swing this deck owns. So a tutor is a kill half, and Nest of Scarabs is the default fetch. A tutor cast for value is the pop-off you didn't have two turns later.

The primary is a pace, not a moment. Nest of Scarabs plus any of nine drains, Yawgmoth working from the zone: one rotation exhausts its own bodies at five to eight activations, roughly two drains per body (stacks 002 and 005), so the table's life falls in installments across turns. Point the counters at their creatures whenever a legal target exists — stacks 002 and 003 measured an opposing two-toughness body extending the rotation by two activations. Free removal and extra fuel, same habit.

Count the library before you go off. The doctor's draw has no "may" in it, so both undying lines end when your library does. The Mikaeus line needs 39 more activations against the 59 your library permits (stack 010). The undying pair — Butcher Ghoul plus Geralf's Messenger — has about 55 activations available and is lethal near 30: each two-activation cycle takes 2 from every opponent and 4 from the seat the Messenger hits, 8 pod life per cycle, at zero net life to you (stack 014). That is roughly twenty-five draws of margin, which is plenty — if you counted first. Announce the loop with the library number in hand; an uncounted loop that eats removal halfway leaves you hellbent over ten cards with no kill in them.

When does the table flip on you? Not when the board gets wide — when a second noncreature payoff resolves. Exquisite Blood. Phyrexian Altar beside a Gravecrawler. Mikaeus untapping. So sequence the loud half last: cheap halves early under the value costume, Nykthos held to convert all those black pips into the engine turn's mana, and the reveal at the end step before your own turn. Count what is open first — "assume every held answer appears the moment you present lethal, and count the table's open mana before committing" (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). Your attempts are cheap by that school's own standard: stack 009 funds its own next cast, stack 011 ends with you at 80 life, stack 014 nets zero. Go. If it fails you kept the board — rebuild and go again.

Expect your quiet to be priced. "Combo decks look non-threatening while advancing in secret, which is exactly why experienced tables hit the quiet ramp player" (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). So never claim you have nothing. Claim the board they can see — the swarm, the drains, the edicts — and sell that as the whole story.

Now the threat that runs the other way, and it is the one to respect. You do not fear a wrath; the drain layer makes a wrath a payment. You fear a two-mana artifact. A resolved Grafdigger's Cage or Cursed Totem covers four of your six kills on a straight oracle reading, and your 99 contains zero cards that destroy or exile an artifact — enumerated across all 80 entries, not estimated. Feed the Swarm destroys a creature or an enchantment an opponent controls, bills you its mana value in life, and touches nothing else. That card plus pressure is the entire out.

So play the artifact hole as politics, because that is what it is. Find the artifact-removal seats at Rule 0 — the green deck, the white deck — and invest in them early: your spot removal on their problems, Grave Pact's edicts on their attackers, your silence on their engines. The day a Cage resolves, their Disenchant is worth more to you than any card you draw. Overpay for it. Until then, pressure the hate player's life total so the lock piece is the card they never untap comfortably behind.

If it sticks anyway, do not shop for the answer you do not own. Pivot the same turn to the shapes that play through it on oracle reading — the Nest engine runs on freshly created tokens and Exquisite Blood never touches a graveyard — and aim the next tutor there. "Name your outs early — the removal or velocity that breaks the piece that beats *you*, not the scariest piece" (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Your outs are named: speed, and somebody else's artifact removal.

At Rule 0, say it straight. Bracket floor 4, forced by four Game Changers and by eleven two-card infinite records. Six rules-verified kill shapes, two unbounded, every one ending all opponents at the same moment. That last sentence is your go decision: you never present lethal to a seat, only to the table. So stop asking whether you can kill somebody. Ask whether what you hold is one of the six shapes, count the open mana, count the library, and go.
matchups:
Assign your seat before your plan, and re-assign it every time the board turns over. Against fair decks you own the long game — act like it. Against anything assembling a lock or a clock faster than your assembly, you are the beatdown, and the polite value plan is how you lose.

THE FAIR, REMOVAL-HEAVY POD is your most common table and your best one. Grind it. Sacrifice on end steps, draw off every body, aim the counters at their creatures, and let Grave Pact turn each activation into an edict no other seat can sell. Mean bodies at turn six is 4.239 and the fodder and drain layers are each 82.3% by turn ten — the machine shows up almost every game, so the missing piece is the only thing worth spending a turn on.

Removal aimed at Yawgmoth here is a trade you accept with a smile: "protection slots and held mana cost you every game, removal only costs you some" (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance). Recast him, bank the goodwill, and save Lightning Greaves, Supernatural Stamina and Malakir Rebirth for the engine turn. Spend the tutors on kill halves — Nest of Scarabs first unless a faster shape is already half-built.

SWEEPER CONTROL is holding a wrath with your name on it. Invite it. Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat and The Meathook Massacre each bill every opponent when a creature you control dies, and Blood Artist bills a chosen seat whenever any creature dies at all — so their sweeper pays you for every body it takes. "Assume the wrath — over a four-player game one is near-certain — so deploy in waves, hold a rebuild package" (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) is your default posture anyway, and your rebuild package is structural: Reassembling Skeleton returns for two forever, Gravecrawler for one, Bitterblossom and Ophiomancer produce a body every upkeep without spending a card.

Hold two mana whenever a control seat untaps with four or more. Plumb the Forbidden turns their announcement into your draw step — sacrifice the board as the additional cost, take a copy per body, and every drain you already have down fires on the way through.

The real exposure sits one permanent type higher. Your kills are piles of permanents and the loops route through noncreature ones — Bastion of Remembrance sits in five verified boards, Exquisite Blood and Phyrexian Altar in others — while all three protection cards save only creatures. So keep the noncreature half of a configuration in hand until the turn it converts, and lead with the halves they will not spend answers on.

STAX AND TAX splits in two, and you must know which half you are sitting in. Against TAXES you are quietly the best-positioned deck at the table, and it is verified rather than vibes: the commander's ability costs no mana, stack 009's Treasure exactly funds the next cast, stack 011's Altar refunds its own black, stack 012 is mandatory and spends nothing, stack 014 nets zero per cycle, and Jet Medallion refunds a tax's first mana before they even charge it. A Sphere halves everyone else's turn and does nothing to a loop already running. Recount your hand, not your board, and deploy each piece the turn you can — the cleaner sequence is not coming.

Against LOCK PERMANENTS you are the worst deck at the table. No artifact answer exists in the 99, so your outs are speed and diplomacy, bought early, as the threat read above coaches. Under a Cursed Totem the creature outlets and the commander's own ability go dark; what remains is the noncreature outlets — Ashnod's Altar, Phyrexian Altar, Blasting Station — and no verified line yet settles what assembles through them alone, so treat that remainder as a lifeline, not a plan. "You rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown, racing the lock's completion" (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Race.

AGGRO thinks a wide board and your 40 life are pressure. They are feeding you. Your three sweepers — Black Sun's Zenith, Soul Snuffers, The Meathook Massacre — all ignite the engine on the way down: you are the one putting the -1/-1 counters on, so Nest of Scarabs pays you an Insect per creature swept, and the Massacre drains as your own bodies die into it. Cast the wipe that leaves you a board.

Spend life like the early points they are — "early points are cheap and late points are priceless" (strategy:life-as-resource). Stack 011 ends with you at 80 and stack 014 costs nothing net, so Necropotence, Black Market Connections and City of Brass are cheap now and priceless later. Switch from spending to defending one turn before it matters, not one after. And an opposing small creature is not even a threat: a two-toughness attacker extends a Nest rotation by two activations (stacks 002 and 003), so point the counters outward and say thank you.

COMBO is your worst seat, so play it with your whole chest. You cannot touch the stack — your instant-speed answers are Deadly Rollick and Fatal Push, both aimed at creatures — so spend them on the enabler the turn it lands. Rollick is free while your commander is out, which is most turns from four on. "Held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now" (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy).

Then race with the shape you can finish, not the one you prefer. Exquisite Blood is your fastest assembly at mean turn 5.085 and reaches 42.6% assembled with a tutor behind it, and the commander's outlet works at instant speed, so once the permanents are down the close does not wait for your main phase. One caution: stack 012's board ignites off South Wind Avatar's own death-trigger lifegain. Marauding Blight-Priest and Starscape Cleric carry the same drain text and gain no life themselves — line up the first lifegain event before you count on either.

GRAVEYARD HATE gets its own read because it splits your kill suite in half on a straight oracle reading. The Gravecrawler loops cast out of the graveyard every iteration and both undying lines return through it, so a resolved Cage effect or crypt-emptier looks lights-out for four shapes — while the Nest engine runs on freshly created tokens and Exquisite Blood never touches a graveyard at all. Nothing verified settles that split yet, so hold it as a working read: under hate, abandon recursion on the spot and tutor toward the Nest engine (38.9% by turn six, assisted) or Exquisite Blood (fastest, mean 5.085). "Know what you can't beat and stop paying for it" (strategy:resource-hedging.playing-to-outs).

You hate back with one land. Bojuka Bog exiles a graveyard on an uncounted land drop — hold it for the turn it strips a reanimation target, not the turn it is convenient. Against a graveyard deck it is the cheapest removal spell you own.
